newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Right rejects plan to join Slovenia government.
newsitem.headline: Right rejects plan to join Slovenia government.

text.p: Slovenia's rightwing parties on Monday rejected a proposal by prime minister-designate Janez Drnovsek to form a coalition government, and told him to go back to the drawing board if he wanted to break the deadlock.

The so-called "Spring" alliance of three rightwing parties told Drnovsek his plan for a unity government had to be redrawn from scratch, saying his proposals did "not recognise the election results and explicitly favours the Liberal Democrats".

Liberal Democrat leader Drnovsek, who won a vote in parliament 10 days ago giving him the mandate to form the next government, needs the backing of at least two of the rightwing parties in order to set up a majority administration.
"We expect that you will prepare a new coalition agreement which will be based on the concept of a government of national unity," the alliance said in a letter to Drnovsek published on Monday.
The new government would be Slovenia's third since independence from Yugoslavia in 1991.
The Liberal Democrats took 25 out of 90 parliamentary seats in an inconclusive November 10 general election.
The "Spring" alliance, comprising the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats, holds 44 seats in the new assembly.
Only two small parties have so far accepted Drnovsek's offer to join a coalition with his centre-right Liberal Democrats -- Desus, a pensioners' party, and the Nationalist Party.
The the United List of Social Democrats, reformed heirs to the communist party, said it still had to consider Drnovsek's proposal.

Drnovsek, who under the constitution has to present his cabinet lineup to parliament by Friday, last week proposed the Liberal Democrats should hold five ministerial posts, the People's Party four and the Social Democrats three cabinet seats.
The Christian Democrats and the United List of Social Democrats would each get two cabinet seats, while the Nationalist Pary and Desus would get one each.
Drnovsek also insisted that the posts of foreign minister and minister of economic affairs would be filled by his party.

But the alliance said the draft lacked clear provisions "regarding the procedures for legislative changes needed prior to European Union entry, particularly for the introduction of protective measures".

Although the "Spring" grouping is not opposed to Slovenia's plan to become a member of the EU by the year 2001, it has called for strong protection of Slovenia's national interests, particularly those of the country's farmers.
